### Abstract
Throughout the female reproductive lifespan, the ovary undergoes hundreds of cycles of follicle development, ovulation and tissue regeneration. How aging disrupts the coordination of such precise, multicellular interactions across time and space is not well understood. Using Slide-seq, a near-cellular spatial transcriptomics method, here we profile 22 mouse ovaries across the reproductive cycle and chronological ages, capturing 610,620 spots across 69 spatial profiles. We develop a novel segmentation pipeline to examine the multicellular dynamics of 358 oocytes, 668 follicles and 236 corpora lutea to find that aging impairs the spatial and temporal coordination required for folliculogenesis even before reproductive cycles cease. These disruptions are characterized by altered immune cell dynamics, inflammatory signaling and global tissue disorganization, which impair the cyclic remodeling required for ovarian function. Our findings reveal how multicellular niches orchestrate ovarian function and demonstrate that age-related breakdown in tissue organization precedes the end of fertility.
Subject terms: Multicellular systems, Computational biology and bioinformatics, Ageing

### Main
The ovary is a highly dynamic organ that undergoes repeated cycles of phenotypic switching to orchestrate oocyte maturation, ovulation and endocrine signaling throughout the reproductive cycle 1 , 2 . This ‘homeostatic cycling’ occurs approximately 150–650 times in mice and 300–400 times in humans throughout the female reproductive lifespan 3 , 4 . Chronological aging leads to a progressive decline in reproductive function, ultimately culminating in the cessation of these cycles. Here we investigate the molecular interactions underlying this transition, focusing on the depletion of the ovarian reserve, the loss of precision in cellular interactions and the accumulation of tissue-wide inflammation and fibrosis 5 – 10 .
Central to ovarian function are follicles, which are multicellular structures that develop growing oocytes and transform into corpora lutea (CL) after ovulation. Folliculogenesis begins with primordial follicles, consisting of a dormant oocyte encased by flattened granulosa cells (GCs). Follicle activation triggers GC proliferation, first forming preantral follicles that undergo morphological and functional changes to support oocyte growth and then transitioning to the gonadotropin-dependent and steroidogenic antral stage 11 , 12 . Notably, less than 1% of recruited follicles reach ovulation while the rest undergo atresia (that is, controlled follicle death) 13 . After ovulation, follicular remnants transform into the CL, a transient progesterone-producing endocrine structure essential for pregnancy and cycle regulation 12 , 14 . Follicle maturation spans multiple reproductive cycles, approximately 18 days in mice and 375 days in humans, creating an extraordinarily complex tissue environment where dozens (mice) or thousands (humans) of follicles at varying developmental stages share the same physical space with multiple CLs 15 , 16 . The molecular mechanisms coordinating such asynchronous spatiotemporal organization remain poorly defined, underscoring 

### Spatial transcriptomics reveals multicellular organization of the cycling and aging ovary
To characterize the multicellular architecture of the ovary, we generated spatial transcriptomics profiles from mice across three reproductive age groups: young (10–12 weeks), middle-aged (36–40 weeks) and old (52–54 weeks) mice 38 . Mice were harvested during the ovulatory (estrus) and post-ovulatory (metestrus) phases, with active cycling confirmed via longitudinal estrous staging (Fig. 1a , Extended Data Fig. 1a , Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 and Methods ). Unsupervised clustering and post hoc annotation resolved all major ovarian cell populations, including oocytes ( Gdf9 ), multiple GC subtypes, theca cells ( Col1a2 ) and two distinct luteal populations ( Parm1 or Akr1c18 ). We also identified epithelial ( Epcam ), fibroblast ( Pdgfra ), smooth muscle ( Tagln ), immune ( Lyz2 ), endothelial ( Flt1 ) and stromal ( Aldh1a1 ) cells (Fig. 1b–d , Extended Data Fig. 1b , Supplementary Tables 3 – 5 and Supplementary Note). To validate these Slide-seq annotations, we also performed whole-ovary single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq). Although snRNA-seq recovered a consistent set of cell types, it showed a notable loss of oocytes and cumulus cells, underscoring the advantage of our spatial profiling for capturing a more comprehensive ovarian cellular atlas (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d ).
Fig. 1. A spatiotemporal map of the cycling and aging ovary identifies spatial niches driving folliculogenesis.
a , Experimental overview. Mice were staged by vaginal cytology and collected at estrus and metestrus ( n = 22; young 10–12 weeks, middle-aged 36–40 weeks, old 52–54 weeks). Multiple nonadjacent sections per ovary were profiled using Slide-seq, with a minimum gap of 200 µm to avoid resampling the same follicle or CL. Adjacent sections were used for histology. After clustering and cell-type annotation, multicellular segments were defined using an automated segmentation pipeline. b , UMAP of Slide-seq RNA profiles ( n = 610,620 dots at 10 µm resolution) across 69 pucks, colored by post h

### Oocytes follow coordinated transcriptional programs during follicular development
Although oocytes are traditionally viewed as transcriptionally silent storage units for maternal RNA 42 , recent evidence reveals active transcriptional regulation throughout their maturation 43 – 45 . Indeed, our in situ profiling of oocyte transcriptomes showed that canonical oocyte marker genes were differentially expressed across their follicle stages (Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ) 31 , 46 – 48 . Further analysis via non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) revealed five distinct oocyte gene programs across their maturation (Fig. 2d , Methods , Extended Data Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ). Oocyte program 2, characterized by zona pellucida glycoproteins genes Zp2 and Zp3 , was upregulated in primordial and preantral oocytes, suggesting the synthesis of components essential for follicular assembly following primordial activation 49 , 50 . In contrast, oocyte program 4, enriched in Bmp15 and F-box proteins genes ( Fbxw19 , Fbxw21 , Fbxw24 ) encoding components of the SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase complex controlling cell cycle progression 51 , 52 , emerged in mature antral oocytes, reflecting shifts required for meiotic progression. In mature oocytes, we observed a significant increase in oocyte program 0 ( Bcl2l10 , Btg4 , Tcl1 ), signaling readiness for growth following the gonadotropin surge (Fig. 2e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0001 preantral versus antral; two-tailed t -test) 53 – 55 . Conversely, atretic oocytes failed to maintain the expression of these programs, showing a loss of Padi6 expression and a premature induction of oocyte program 0 (Fig. 2a,e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0203 antral versus atretic; two-tailed t -test). Altogether, our findings reveal that oocyte transcription may be dynamically regulated throughout folliculogenesis to govern the switch from oocyte dormancy to maturation.

### Molecular programs define spatially organized follicle lifecycles in young ovaries
Next, we investigated how GC states change throughout folliculogenesis. To compare GC organization across hundreds of follicles of varying sizes, we devised a normalized, scaled radial distance from the follicle center. Quantifying GC composition along this radial axis revealed extensive intra-follicle heterogeneity, indicating that transitions between follicle stages are not driven by a synchronized follicle-wide switch, but instead may emerge through the local propagation of changes in cell–cell interactions (Fig. 3a,b , Extended Data Fig. 3a , Supplementary Table 6 and Methods ).
Fig. 3. Spatiotemporal coordination of GCs within the follicular niche.
a , Representative spatial plot showing follicular cell types (colors), including preantral, antral early mitotic, antral mitotic, antral luteinizing and atretic GC subtypes, alongside oocyte and theca cell spots. b , Radial distribution of GC subtypes (colored lines, y axis) across follicle types (panels). Lines indicate mean proportion of each subtype across 10 scaled radial bins ( x axis; 0, follicle center; 1, edge); shading, s.e.m. across follicles. Significant monotonic radial trends are indicated (preantral follicles: GC—preantral * P = 0.0283, antral mitotic follicles: GC—antral mitotic * P = 0.0479, GC—antral luteinizing * P = 0.0479, antral luteinizing follicles: GC—antral luteinizing * P = 0.0045, atretic follicles: GC—atretic * P &lt; 0.0001, two-sided Spearman correlation). n = 653 follicles from 22 mice, all ages; follicle counts by type in Supplementary Table 6 . c , Spatial organization of GC cell cycle states. Left: representative spatial plot with cycling (G2M/S, pink) and non-cycling (G1, gray) GCs. Right: mean radial distribution of cycling vs non-cycling GCs ( y axis); shading, s.e.m. across follicles. Significant monotonic trends indicated (cycling: * P &lt; 0.0001, non-cycling: * P &lt; 0.0001, two-sided Spearman correlation; n = 668 follicles). d , Diffusion pseudotime (DPT) across non-atretic

### Aging disrupts the temporal trajectory of GC differentiation and alters atresia progression
Analysis of transcriptional programs across the follicular lifecycle revealed that aging disrupts the coordinated molecular transitions observed across granulosa cell differentiation. In young ovaries, GEP usage across GC trajectories defined by DPT and follicle type follow an ordered progression: GCs in preantral follicles initiate an early development program (GEP9; Wt1, Wnt4 ), progress through proliferative expansion (GEP3; Top2a , Mki67 ) in antral, followed by the induction of follicular dominance (GEP2 and GEP4; Inhbb , Fst ; Esr2 , Greb1l ) and luteinization (GEP1; Lhcgr , Hsd3b1 ) programs heightened at metestrus (Fig. 3h , Extended Data Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Table 12 ). Atretic follicles are characterized by apoptosis-associated programs (GEP10 and GEP11; Thbs1 , Pik3ip1 ; Ghr, Ptprd ) (Fig. 3h , Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 12 ). In contrast, aged ovaries displayed altered timing and intensity of GEPs, indicating a breakdown in the normal sequence of GC state transitions across follicle development (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 3h ). For example, aged antral follicles downregulate the luteinization program (GEP1) (Fig. 3h,i , Extended Data Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Table 12 ). Notably, atretic follicles were the most affected by aging, with decreased canonical apoptosis-associated programs (GEP10 and GEP11) and aberrant upregulation of the ECM remodeling program (GEP6; Col1a2 , Lama2 ), which is typically specific to preantral follicles in young ovaries. These patterns suggest an age-associated shift from regulated to dysregulated remodeling of the follicular niche, resulting in a ‘molecular blurring’ between the boundaries of developmental and degenerative processes.

### Multicellular dynamics and interactions shaping folliculogenesis progression
Folliculogenesis is driven by coordinated interactions across multiple cell types, extending beyond cell-intrinsic granulosa programs. To resolve this higher-order organization (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6 ), we ordered follicle segments from reproductively young mice along a computationally inferred trajectory of folliculogenesis (Fig. 4b,c and Supplementary Table 6 ), visualized in a UMAP embedding (Fig. 4d , Extended Data Fig. 4a , Supplementary Tables 6 and 15 and Methods ). Diffusion pseudotime recapitulated canonical transitions from preantral to antral or atretic follicles (Fig. 4e ), accompanied by progressive shifts in cell type composition (Extended Data Fig. 4b ). To link these compositional changes to intercellular signaling, we applied MultiNicheNet 85 to infer receptor-ligand interactions among oocytes, granulosa, theca and immune cells ( Methods and Extended Data Fig. 4c ). This analysis revealed follicle stage-specific communication patterns, including Gdf9 - Fxyd6 between oocytes and GCs in preantral follicles, Fst - Bmpr1b between granulosa and theca cells in antral follicles, and Apoa4 - Lrp1 within GCs in atretic follicles (Fig. 4f , Supplementary Table 16 and Methods ). The atretic-enriched Apoa4-Lrp1 interaction implicated metabolic reprogramming during follicle regression: Lrp1 regulates lipid transport and glucose metabolism 86 , 87 , whereas Apoa4 promotes lipid handling and facilitates glucose uptake 88 . Notably, LRP1 has been genetically associated with polycystic ovarian syndrome, a disorder characterized by metabolic and endocrine dysfunction 89 . Together, these results indicate that dynamic, stage-specific intercellular signaling coordinates follicle progression.
Fig. 4. Aging disrupts temporal coupling in folliculogenesis.
a , Mean cell-type composition across preantral ( n = 238), antral mitotic ( n = 191), atretic ( n = 181) and antral luteinizing ( n = 43) follicles, and CL ( n = 234). b , Schematic of optimal transport infe

### Dysregulation of CL clearance with aging may initiate inflammatory remodeling
We next examined whether the dynamics of the post-ovulatory luteal cells are also altered with age. Identification of two spatially segregated luteal cell populations with opposing progesterone regulatory programs suggested a temporal phenotypic switch during the luteal lifecycle. Parm1 -enriched CLs (‘CL – Parm1’) express progesterone synthesis genes, contain vascular endothelial cells, are enriched at estrus and consist of histologically smaller cells 92 , 93 , features consistent with newly formed, hormonally active CLs 14 , 32 , 94 – 96 . In contrast, Akr1c18 -enriched CLs (‘CL – Akr1c18’) express the luteal regression marker Ptgfr , are infiltrated by immune cells, are more frequent at metestrus and contain histologically larger cells 92 , 93 , features consistent with luteolysis and regression (Fig. 5a–c , Extended Data Fig. 5a–f and Supplementary Tables 4 , 6 and 17 ) 96 . In aged ovaries, although these transcriptional distinctions between luteal subtypes were preserved (Extended Data Fig. 5g ), Akr1c18 CLs were significantly accumulated at estrus compared to young ovaries (Fig. 5b , P = 0.0055, two-tailed t -test; Supplementary Table 17 ), suggesting failed timely clearance. Because timely CL regression and the accompanying drop in progesterone are required to initiate the next cycle 14 , 95 , 97 , persistence of these degenerating CLs likely disrupts progesterone homeostasis, potentially impairing cycle progression 1 , 11 .
Fig. 5. Aging disrupts CL clearance.
a , Fluorescence in situ hybridization of Parm1 (yellow) and Akr1c18 (teal) in a young ovary. Scale bar, 100 µm. Representative result across four replicates. b , Fraction of each CL type per puck ( y axis) during estrus across age groups ( x axis) for individual pucks (dots) and mean across pucks (bars). Error bars represent standard deviation across pucks (young n = 23, old n = 12), and significance was determined by two-tailed t -test. c , Cell type composition of CL subtypes. Boxplots show spot c

### Spatial immune remodeling reveals multiple drivers of ovarian inflammaging
To define how aging reshapes global immune organization 7 , 28 , we characterized the composition and spatial architecture of immune populations across the ovary. First, we identified key immune subpopulations, including four macrophage subsets (phagocytic, antigen-presenting, efferocytic and metabolically active), dendritic cells, mast cells, plasma cells and T cells, each occupying distinct spatial niches (Fig. 6a,b , Supplementary Tables 6 , 17 and 19 and Supplementary Note ). Phagocytic and antigen-presenting macrophages (macrophages 1 and 2) were the dominant populations and expanded preferentially in preantral and atretic follicles, and in CLs, with age (Fig. 6b,c and Supplementary Tables 15 and 17 ). Across all ages, phagocytic macrophages (macrophage 1) localized to the periphery of follicles and CLs, whereas antigen-presenting macrophages (macrophage 2) concentrated toward follicular and CL centers, a compartmentalization accentuated in aged ovaries (Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 15 ). Immunofluorescence of regressing CLs confirmed CD11b + macrophage and CD3 + T cell accumulation in these central niches, suggesting their cooperative role in antigen presentation during luteal clearance (Fig. 6f ). Although low in abundance, the expansion of T cells in aged CLs (Fig. 6c ; P = 0.0079, two-tailed t -test) may represent the anatomical location underlying prior reports of cytotoxic and double negative T cells accumulation in the aging mouse ovary 34 . Altogether, these data reveal that ovarian aging involves coordinated remodeling of multiple immune niches, pointing to spatially coexisting immune programs that may jointly drive ovarian inflammaging.
Fig. 6. Age-associated changes in immune composition.

### MNGCs define a specialized macrophage fusion pathology in aging ovaries
Among age-expanded immune niches, multinucleated giant cells (MNGCs) emerged as a distinct macrophage-associated pathology. Accumulation of MNGCs is a hallmark of ovarian aging associated with chronic inflammation and fibrosis 8 , 28 , 98 , 99 , visible as fused cellular clusters on H&amp;E sections (Fig. 7a,b and Extended Data Fig. 6a ). Registering adjacent H&amp;E sections to Slide-seq pucks using anatomical landmarks enabled comparing immune spots located within versus outside MNGCs (Fig. 7c , Extended Data Fig. 6b and Methods ), which revealed an enrichment of phagocytic macrophages within MNGCs (Fig. 7d ). Across macrophage subpopulations, those within MNGCs adopted specialized transcriptional programs distinct from the surrounding stroma, including complement- and fusion-associated genes ( Tagln , Acta2, Itgae ) in antigen-presenting macrophages, clearance programs in efferocytic macrophages ( Gpnmb , Mfge8 , Ctsd ) and inflammatory-lipid remodeling signatures in metabolically active macrophages ( Pla2g7 , Lyz2 , Lgals3 ) (Fig. 7e , Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Table 20 ). Together, these findings suggest that MNGCs represent specialized inflammatory fusion niches underlying defective tissue clearance, potentially linking immune dysfunction to fibrotic pathology.
Fig. 7. Global changes in tissue-wide remodeling with aging.
a , Representative H&amp;E section showing multinucleated giant cells (MNGCs) in aged ovaries, with manually annotated MNGC masks. b , Distribution of histology sections ( y axis) classified as MNGC-high or MNGC-low across young ( n = 31), middle ( n = 16) and old ( n = 21) pucks ( x axis). c , Representative registration of MNGC masks from adjacent H&amp;E to Slide-seq using Napari; spots are colored by annotated cell type (colors). d , Mean proportions of immune cell subtypes within MNGC regions in old ( n = 21) pucks. e , log 2 fold changes of representative genes across macrophage subsets (rows) comparing stromal macrophages 

### Aging disrupts interfollicular spatial coupling
Age-associated immune remodeling converged with broader stromal disorganization, suggesting organ-level consequences of inflammaging. Across stromal populations residing outside of follicles and CL, we observed a progressive expansion of surface epithelial and immune populations, accompanied by depletion of steroidogenic stromal cells 7 , 100 – 103 (Fig. 7f , compositional test with scCODA 104 ; Extended Data Fig. 6d ; Supplementary Table 5 ; and Methods ). Thickening of the surface epithelium was independently confirmed by morphometric measurements on adjacent H&amp;E sections (Extended Data Fig. 6e and Methods ). Cell type compositional shifts coincided with transcriptional changes marked by reduced expression of ECM genes and increased metalloproteases that may indicate aberrant ECM remodeling, as well as elevated fibrotic and inflammatory signatures 100 (Fig. 7g , Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Tables 21 and 22 ).

### Discussion
Here we present a near-cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the naturally cycling murine ovary across reproductive ages and show that ovarian aging is characterized by the progressive erosion of multiscale spatiotemporal tissue organization. Across cellular, niche and tissue scales, aging disrupted spatial patterning within follicles, temporal coordination of folliculogenesis and CL turnover, and immune–stromal homeostasis, with changes emerging before cessation of cycling. These findings indicate that reproductive aging can be viewed as a progressive breakdown of tissue-level coordination, rather than solely the depletion of the follicle reserve.
Our findings suggest that the spatial organization of follicles is an elegant mechanism for survival and resource allocation. By compartmentalizing proliferative activity to inner GCs and hormone-sensing, steroidogenic functions to outer GCs positioned near the vasculature and stroma, follicles optimize resource allocation under the energetic constraints of this competitive environment. We hypothesize that successful spatial compartmentalization of GC function during folliculogenesis could contribute to follicular fate, with dominant follicles effectively maintaining functional polarity, whereas less efficient competitors undergo atresia 107 , 108 . More broadly, our findings refine a view of follicular atresia as a heterogeneous process linked to metabolic, immune and tissue remodeling programs, rather than a uniform degenerative endpoint. Although our results suggest a plausible sequence of atresia commitment arising from multiple GC lineages, the specific molecular drivers remain to be experimentally validated 109 – 112 . In aged ovaries, the blurring of developmental and degenerative boundaries points to compromised follicle viability. Whether atretic fate is caused primarily by oocyte-intrinsic cues or by a dysregulated follicular environment remains unclear.

### Estrous cycle staging mice by vaginal cytology
Mice collected at UCSF were staged near-daily for 8 consecutive days using vaginal cytology, as previously described 118 , 119 . A total volume of 100 µl sterile saline (in 20–50 µl increments) was expelled five to ten times with a P200 pipette into the vaginal canal, taking care to avoid touching the vaginal opening with the pipette tip then expelled onto a glass slide and imaged immediately using Nikon Eclipse Ts2 (10× objective) and a Nikon DS Qi2 camera. Broad and Yale mice
Female mice were staged near-daily for 8 consecutive days using vaginal cytology, as previously described 118 , 119 . Briefly, mini-tip flocked nasopharyngeal swabs (VWR SLIN501CS01) were moistened with sterile PBS, and approximately one-fourth of the flocked tip was inserted into the vaginal canal of manually restrained mice. Swabs were rotated five times clockwise and five times counterclockwise and then smeared onto a non-treated glass slide (VWR 16004-422). Slides were air-dried and stained with a 0.1% crystal violet solution (Jorgenson J0322) for 1–2 min. Excess stain was rinsed with PBS and sterile water, and the slides were counterstained with 1% eosin (Jorgenson #J0322A) for 10–20 s. Following the counterstaining step, slides were rinsed again, air-dried completely, examined under a light microscope and imaged with a Leica Aperio VERSA Brightfield, Fluorescence &amp; FISH Digital Pathology Scanner, using the 20× objective.

### In situ transcriptome processing via Slide-seq
Tissue sections were processed and sequenced using Slide-seq v2 as previously described 36 . Slide-seq arrays were purchased from Curio Biosciences (Curio Seeker) or prepared in-house using custom-synthesized barcoded beads functionalized with the sequence 25 (5′TTT_PC_GCCGGTAATACGACTCACTATAGGGCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCTJJJJJJJJTCTTCAGCGTTCCCGAGAJJJJJJNNNNNNNVVT30-3′) with a photocleavable linker (PC), a bead barcode sequence (J, 14 bp), a UMI sequence (NNNNNNNVV, 9 bp) and a poly dT tail. The sample table of all Slide-seq data, denoting the puck origin and other metadata, is in Supplementary Table 2 .

### Initial data processing
Gene expression data of individual samples or pucks were concatenated using an outer join. For spatial data, spatial coordinates were assigned by matching barcodes to puck-specific barcode mapping files. The combined dataset was filtered to retain spots with at least 50 detected genes and 150 UMI counts. For spot clustering and embeddings, all gene expression values were scaled and centered, and the top 5,000 highly variable genes were identified from log-normalized counts across batches using Scanpy’s highly_variable_genes function (batch Key=puck) 124 . Dimensionality reduction was performed by regressing out total UMI counts, followed by principal component analysis (PCA) on highly variable genes. Puck-specific batch effects were corrected using a PyTorch implementation of Harmony 125 , after which a k-nearest-neighbor graph with 10 neighbors was constructed using the top 40 principal components. Unsupervised spot clusters were identified using the Leiden algorithm 126 (resolution = 1.5) and visualized using UMAP 127 , implemented in Scanpy 124 (v1.10.1).

### Projection of additional pucks onto the annotated reference atlas
To incorporate newly generated Slide-seq pucks (young, metestrus) into the reference atlas, raw gene-by-spot matrices were preprocessed as described above, including spatial coordinate assignment and smear removal. To ensure compatibility with the reference atlas, gene sets were harmonized prior to integration by restricting the query AnnData object to the intersection of genes shared between query and reference. The cleaned query data were projected onto the existing atlas using scvi-tools (v1.1.6), leveraging a pretrained SCVI model to infer a shared representation. Latent embeddings for the query were obtained and concatenated with reference embeddings for downstream analysis.

### Subclustering of immune cells and GCs
To refine cell state annotation, we performed iterative subclustering of immune cells and GCs. AnnData objects were subset to populations of interest, normalized to 10,000 transcripts per cell with highly expressed genes down-weighted (max_fraction = 0.05), log-transformed and scaled to unit variance. Highly variable genes were identified using Scanpy’s highly_variable_genes function (flavor = ‘seurat’, batch_key = ‘segment_label’), followed by PCA and neighborhood graph construction. UMAP was used for visualization and Leiden clustering for subcluster identification. DEGs were identified for each subcluster using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (min log fold-change ≥ 1). Marker genes used for annotation were required to be (i) specific to the cluster, (ii) highly expressed within that cluster and (iii) supported by prior literature as having cell-type-defining functional roles.

### Spatial segmentation of oocytes, follicles and CL
Code underlying these analyses can be found in II.2_segmentation.ipynb and II.3_segment_extension.ipynb.
‘Oocyte’ and ‘Oocyte - cumulus’ clusters were initially used as putative oocyte spots to account for uncertainty at cluster boundaries in space. For each puck, a spatial neighborhood graph (radius = 50) was constructed and clustered using Leiden 126 (resolution = 0.1) to define preliminary oocyte segments. ‘Oocyte - cumulus’ spots were subsequently removed, and segments containing fewer than three spots were excluded. Segments were further refined by subclustering, merging and manual curation based on tissue context. Decontamination of cumulus signals from oocytes
To remove residual cumulus contamination from oocytes, NMF 136 was applied iteratively to oocyte spots using scikit-learn 137 ( k = 8 programs). Programs associated with contaminating signals were identified by marker genes, and spots were annotated as contaminants if they either had these programs as their top utilized program or if the program scores reached the following thresholds: Program 1 ( Kctd14 , Slc18a2 , Wt1 ): &gt; 0.4, Program 2 ( Lars2 , Hexb , Cdk8 ): &gt; 0.3, Program 4 ( Inhba , Inhbb , Nap1l5 ): &gt; 0.3, Program 6 ( Col1a2 , Col3a1 , Cfh ): &gt; 0.4 (Supplementary Fig. 3a,b ). Contaminating spots were removed across two rounds of filtering; in the second round, spots with program 1 ( Serpine2 , Ccnd2 , Kctd14 ) as the top program or with a score &gt;0.3 were annotated as contaminants (Supplementary Fig. 3c,d ) and removed from the oocyte segments. Identifying primordial oocytes
To capture small, putatively primordial, oocytes, unassigned ‘Oocyte’ spots or spots expressing Sohlh1 31 , 138 located at least 200 from existing oocyte segment centers were selected. For pucks containing at least two such spots, a neighborhood graph (radius 20 µm) was clustered using Leiden 124 clustering (resolution = 0.1). Segments with less than 2 spots or lacking Sohlh1 expression were excluded. Segmenta

### Identifying gene programs with non-negative factorization
Gene programs in composite oocytes were identified using NMF ( k = 5) in scikit-learn 136 , 137 on log-normalized counts. Gene rank per program was determined by the gene weight matrix. GCs

### Analysis of GEPs with pseudotime (DPT)
To investigate transcriptional dynamics during follicle development and atresia, GC GEP usage scores were analyzed along DPT, computed as a unified trajectory across all GC spots. Stage stream plots depict follicle type occupancy along pseudotime, estimated using Gaussian kernel density estimates over 400 grid points and displayed as stacked area plots. Estrous stage occupancy (second row, where available) was computed similarly. GEP heatmaps were generated separately for non-atretic and atretic by binning pseudotime into 500 equal-width intervals and calculating mean GEP usage per bin.
Age-associated differences in GEP usage were tested within each GEP, follicle type and estrous stage using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with cluster-robust standard errors (Usage_k ~ age; young as reference), clustering variance by puck to account for within-puck dependence of spots. Strata lacking both age groups were not estimable. Across all tested GEP × follicle type × stage combinations, P values were adjusted for multiple testing (Benjamini–Hochberg; significance set at FDR &lt; 0.05). Analyses were performed using statsmodels (statsmodels.formula.api.ols, statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests).

### Compositional analysis of cell and segment types
Global cell-type compositional analysis
Cell-type composition was calculated as the fraction of spots assigned to each cell type within each puck, and then averaged across young, middle and old groups. Age-associated compositional changes were tested using scCODA 143 , with young as the reference condition, and ‘Epithelial – oviduct’ as the reference cell type because of its low variability across conditions. Immune subsets were additionally stratified by segment assignments (follicle, CL or stroma if unassigned). CL-associated endothelial cells were analyzed separately from other endothelial cells. Cell-type composition within segments
Within each segment, cell-type composition was calculated as the fraction of spots assigned to each cell type, and then averaged across segment types. To test age-associated differences within follicle types, proportions were transformed using a centered log-ratio and modeled using OLS regression (centered log-ratio ~ age) with cluster-robust standard errors by puck to account for within-sample correlation. As before, P values were adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing (Benjamini–Hochberg; significance, FDR &lt; 0.10). Segment-type composition analysis

### Follicle embedding and trajectory inference using optimal transport
Code for these analyses is in III_segment_OT_1_pca_coretypes.ipynb and III_segment_OT_2_plot_results.ipynb.
Segment-to-segment distance matrix computation
Pairwise distances between all follicle and CL segments in young mice were computed using optimal transport, with each segment represented by its oocyte, granulosa or luteal, and theca spots. For each segment pair, a transport matrix was estimated using the Sinkhorn algorithm implemented in moscot 144 (epsilon = 0, tau_a = 1, tau_b = 1, rank = 20, initializer = k-means, min_iterations = 5, max_iterations = 200). Segment distance was defined as the sum of the element-wise product of the transport matrix and the corresponding cost matrix of the optimal transport problem. Segment embedding and follicle pseudotime
The resulting segment-to-segment distance matrix used as a feature space for embedding. A k-nearest neighbor graph ( k = 15) was constructed from the top 50 PCs and visualized using UMAP. Embeddings were generated for all follicle and CL segments in young mice, as well as follicles alone in young mice as the reference trajectory. DPT 139 was then computed for young follicles using a manually selected root segment. Trajectory projection of follicles from middle-aged and old mice

### Cell–cell communication analysis
Code for these analyses is in III.5_nichenet_ageYoung_stageAll_segmentFollicle_withOocyte_byCluster.Rmd and III_segment_OT_2_plot_results_v0.3.ipynb.

### Age-associated differential gene expression analysis
For follicular hormone-response genes, mean expression and s.e.m. were calculated within each follicle type (preantral, antral mitotic, antral luteinizing and atretic), estrous stage (estrus, metestrus) and age group for Amhr2 , Fshr and Lhcgr 8 , 28 , 98 , 99 , 145 . Differential expression between estrous stages was performed using two-sided t -tests. Oocytes and stromal cells

### Identifying MNGCs
Code for these analyses is in II.5_registration_v0.8_all_pucks.ipynb and III_MNGC_dotplot_v0.1.ipynb.
Annotation of MNGCs in histology sections
Adjacent H&amp;E-stained sections were manually annotated for MNGCs based on pigmentation, size and proximity to growing follicles, as previously described 8 , 28 , 98 , 99 , 146 . Sections were classified as ‘visible MNGCs’ (high density of light brown clusters; n = 19), ‘possible MNGCs’ (lower density or weaker pigmentation; n = 13) or ‘no MNGCs.’ MNGC segmentation in registered spatial transcriptomics data

### Abstract
Throughout the female reproductive lifespan, the ovary undergoes hundreds of cycles of follicle development, ovulation and tissue regeneration. How aging disrupts the coordination of such precise, multicellular interactions across time and space is not well understood. Using Slide-seq, a near-cellular spatial transcriptomics method, here we profile 22 mouse ovaries across the reproductive cycle and chronological ages, capturing 610,620 spots across 69 spatial profiles. We develop a novel segmentation pipeline to examine the multicellular dynamics of 358 oocytes, 668 follicles and 236 corpora lutea to find that aging impairs the spatial and temporal coordination required for folliculogenesis even before reproductive cycles cease. These disruptions are characterized by altered immune cell dynamics, inflammatory signaling and global tissue disorganization, which impair the cyclic remodeling required for ovarian function. Our findings reveal how multicellular niches orchestrate ovarian function and demonstrate that age-related breakdown in tissue organization precedes the end of fertility.
Subject terms: Multicellular systems, Computational biology and bioinformatics, Ageing

### Main
The ovary is a highly dynamic organ that undergoes repeated cycles of phenotypic switching to orchestrate oocyte maturation, ovulation and endocrine signaling throughout the reproductive cycle 1 , 2 . This ‘homeostatic cycling’ occurs approximately 150–650 times in mice and 300–400 times in humans throughout the female reproductive lifespan 3 , 4 . Chronological aging leads to a progressive decline in reproductive function, ultimately culminating in the cessation of these cycles. Here we investigate the molecular interactions underlying this transition, focusing on the depletion of the ovarian reserve, the loss of precision in cellular interactions and the accumulation of tissue-wide inflammation and fibrosis 5 – 10 .
Central to ovarian function are follicles, which are multicellular structures that develop growing oocytes and transform into corpora lutea (CL) after ovulation. Folliculogenesis begins with primordial follicles, consisting of a dormant oocyte encased by flattened granulosa cells (GCs). Follicle activation triggers GC proliferation, first forming preantral follicles that undergo morphological and functional changes to support oocyte growth and then transitioning to the gonadotropin-dependent and steroidogenic antral stage 11 , 12 . Notably, less than 1% of recruited follicles reach ovulation while the rest undergo atresia (that is, controlled follicle death) 13 . After ovulation, follicular remnants transform into the CL, a transient progesterone-producing endocrine structure essential for pregnancy and cycle regulation 12 , 14 . Follicle maturation spans multiple reproductive cycles, approximately 18 days in mice and 375 days in humans, creating an extraordinarily complex tissue environment where dozens (mice) or thousands (humans) of follicles at varying developmental stages share the same physical space with multiple CLs 15 , 16 . The molecular mechanisms coordinating such asynchronous spatiotemporal organization remain poorly defined, underscoring 

### Spatial transcriptomics reveals multicellular organization of the cycling and aging ovary
To characterize the multicellular architecture of the ovary, we generated spatial transcriptomics profiles from mice across three reproductive age groups: young (10–12 weeks), middle-aged (36–40 weeks) and old (52–54 weeks) mice 38 . Mice were harvested during the ovulatory (estrus) and post-ovulatory (metestrus) phases, with active cycling confirmed via longitudinal estrous staging (Fig. 1a , Extended Data Fig. 1a , Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 and Methods ). Unsupervised clustering and post hoc annotation resolved all major ovarian cell populations, including oocytes ( Gdf9 ), multiple GC subtypes, theca cells ( Col1a2 ) and two distinct luteal populations ( Parm1 or Akr1c18 ). We also identified epithelial ( Epcam ), fibroblast ( Pdgfra ), smooth muscle ( Tagln ), immune ( Lyz2 ), endothelial ( Flt1 ) and stromal ( Aldh1a1 ) cells (Fig. 1b–d , Extended Data Fig. 1b , Supplementary Tables 3 – 5 and Supplementary Note). To validate these Slide-seq annotations, we also performed whole-ovary single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq). Although snRNA-seq recovered a consistent set of cell types, it showed a notable loss of oocytes and cumulus cells, underscoring the advantage of our spatial profiling for capturing a more comprehensive ovarian cellular atlas (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d ).

### Oocytes follow coordinated transcriptional programs during follicular development
Although oocytes are traditionally viewed as transcriptionally silent storage units for maternal RNA 42 , recent evidence reveals active transcriptional regulation throughout their maturation 43 – 45 . Indeed, our in situ profiling of oocyte transcriptomes showed that canonical oocyte marker genes were differentially expressed across their follicle stages (Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ) 31 , 46 – 48 . Further analysis via non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) revealed five distinct oocyte gene programs across their maturation (Fig. 2d , Methods , Extended Data Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ). Oocyte program 2, characterized by zona pellucida glycoproteins genes Zp2 and Zp3 , was upregulated in primordial and preantral oocytes, suggesting the synthesis of components essential for follicular assembly following primordial activation 49 , 50 . In contrast, oocyte program 4, enriched in Bmp15 and F-box proteins genes ( Fbxw19 , Fbxw21 , Fbxw24 ) encoding components of the SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase complex controlling cell cycle progression 51 , 52 , emerged in mature antral oocytes, reflecting shifts required for meiotic progression. In mature oocytes, we observed a significant increase in oocyte program 0 ( Bcl2l10 , Btg4 , Tcl1 ), signaling readiness for growth following the gonadotropin surge (Fig. 2e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0001 preantral versus antral; two-tailed t -test) 53 – 55 . Conversely, atretic oocytes failed to maintain the expression of these programs, showing a loss of Padi6 expression and a premature induction of oocyte program 0 (Fig. 2a,e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0203 antral versus atretic; two-tailed t -test). Altogether, our findings reveal that oocyte transcription may be dynamically regulated throughout folliculogenesis to govern the switch from oocyte dormancy to maturation.

### Molecular programs define spatially organized follicle lifecycles in young ovaries
Next, we investigated how GC states change throughout folliculogenesis. To compare GC organization across hundreds of follicles of varying sizes, we devised a normalized, scaled radial distance from the follicle center. Quantifying GC composition along this radial axis revealed extensive intra-follicle heterogeneity, indicating that transitions between follicle stages are not driven by a synchronized follicle-wide switch, but instead may emerge through the local propagation of changes in cell–cell interactions (Fig. 3a,b , Extended Data Fig. 3a , Supplementary Table 6 and Methods ).

### Aging disrupts the temporal trajectory of GC differentiation and alters atresia progression
Analysis of transcriptional programs across the follicular lifecycle revealed that aging disrupts the coordinated molecular transitions observed across granulosa cell differentiation. In young ovaries, GEP usage across GC trajectories defined by DPT and follicle type follow an ordered progression: GCs in preantral follicles initiate an early development program (GEP9; Wt1, Wnt4 ), progress through proliferative expansion (GEP3; Top2a , Mki67 ) in antral, followed by the induction of follicular dominance (GEP2 and GEP4; Inhbb , Fst ; Esr2 , Greb1l ) and luteinization (GEP1; Lhcgr , Hsd3b1 ) programs heightened at metestrus (Fig. 3h , Extended Data Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Table 12 ). Atretic follicles are characterized by apoptosis-associated programs (GEP10 and GEP11; Thbs1 , Pik3ip1 ; Ghr, Ptprd ) (Fig. 3h , Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 12 ). In contrast, aged ovaries displayed altered timing and intensity of GEPs, indicating a breakdown in the normal sequence of GC state transitions across follicle development (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 3h ). For example, aged antral follicles downregulate the luteinization program (GEP1) (Fig. 3h,i , Extended Data Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Table 12 ). Notably, atretic follicles were the most affected by aging, with decreased canonical apoptosis-associated programs (GEP10 and GEP11) and aberrant upregulation of the ECM remodeling program (GEP6; Col1a2 , Lama2 ), which is typically specific to preantral follicles in young ovaries. These patterns suggest an age-associated shift from regulated to dysregulated remodeling of the follicular niche, resulting in a ‘molecular blurring’ between the boundaries of developmental and degenerative processes.

### Multicellular dynamics and interactions shaping folliculogenesis progression
Folliculogenesis is driven by coordinated interactions across multiple cell types, extending beyond cell-intrinsic granulosa programs. To resolve this higher-order organization (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6 ), we ordered follicle segments from reproductively young mice along a computationally inferred trajectory of folliculogenesis (Fig. 4b,c and Supplementary Table 6 ), visualized in a UMAP embedding (Fig. 4d , Extended Data Fig. 4a , Supplementary Tables 6 and 15 and Methods ). Diffusion pseudotime recapitulated canonical transitions from preantral to antral or atretic follicles (Fig. 4e ), accompanied by progressive shifts in cell type composition (Extended Data Fig. 4b ). To link these compositional changes to intercellular signaling, we applied MultiNicheNet 85 to infer receptor-ligand interactions among oocytes, granulosa, theca and immune cells ( Methods and Extended Data Fig. 4c ). This analysis revealed follicle stage-specific communication patterns, including Gdf9 - Fxyd6 between oocytes and GCs in preantral follicles, Fst - Bmpr1b between granulosa and theca cells in antral follicles, and Apoa4 - Lrp1 within GCs in atretic follicles (Fig. 4f , Supplementary Table 16 and Methods ). The atretic-enriched Apoa4-Lrp1 interaction implicated metabolic reprogramming during follicle regression: Lrp1 regulates lipid transport and glucose metabolism 86 , 87 , whereas Apoa4 promotes lipid handling and facilitates glucose uptake 88 . Notably, LRP1 has been genetically associated with polycystic ovarian syndrome, a disorder characterized by metabolic and endocrine dysfunction 89 . Together, these results indicate that dynamic, stage-specific intercellular signaling coordinates follicle progression.

### Dysregulation of CL clearance with aging may initiate inflammatory remodeling
We next examined whether the dynamics of the post-ovulatory luteal cells are also altered with age. Identification of two spatially segregated luteal cell populations with opposing progesterone regulatory programs suggested a temporal phenotypic switch during the luteal lifecycle. Parm1 -enriched CLs (‘CL – Parm1’) express progesterone synthesis genes, contain vascular endothelial cells, are enriched at estrus and consist of histologically smaller cells 92 , 93 , features consistent with newly formed, hormonally active CLs 14 , 32 , 94 – 96 . In contrast, Akr1c18 -enriched CLs (‘CL – Akr1c18’) express the luteal regression marker Ptgfr , are infiltrated by immune cells, are more frequent at metestrus and contain histologically larger cells 92 , 93 , features consistent with luteolysis and regression (Fig. 5a–c , Extended Data Fig. 5a–f and Supplementary Tables 4 , 6 and 17 ) 96 . In aged ovaries, although these transcriptional distinctions between luteal subtypes were preserved (Extended Data Fig. 5g ), Akr1c18 CLs were significantly accumulated at estrus compared to young ovaries (Fig. 5b , P = 0.0055, two-tailed t -test; Supplementary Table 17 ), suggesting failed timely clearance. Because timely CL regression and the accompanying drop in progesterone are required to initiate the next cycle 14 , 95 , 97 , persistence of these degenerating CLs likely disrupts progesterone homeostasis, potentially impairing cycle progression 1 , 11 .

### Spatial immune remodeling reveals multiple drivers of ovarian inflammaging
To define how aging reshapes global immune organization 7 , 28 , we characterized the composition and spatial architecture of immune populations across the ovary. First, we identified key immune subpopulations, including four macrophage subsets (phagocytic, antigen-presenting, efferocytic and metabolically active), dendritic cells, mast cells, plasma cells and T cells, each occupying distinct spatial niches (Fig. 6a,b , Supplementary Tables 6 , 17 and 19 and Supplementary Note ). Phagocytic and antigen-presenting macrophages (macrophages 1 and 2) were the dominant populations and expanded preferentially in preantral and atretic follicles, and in CLs, with age (Fig. 6b,c and Supplementary Tables 15 and 17 ). Across all ages, phagocytic macrophages (macrophage 1) localized to the periphery of follicles and CLs, whereas antigen-presenting macrophages (macrophage 2) concentrated toward follicular and CL centers, a compartmentalization accentuated in aged ovaries (Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 15 ). Immunofluorescence of regressing CLs confirmed CD11b + macrophage and CD3 + T cell accumulation in these central niches, suggesting their cooperative role in antigen presentation during luteal clearance (Fig. 6f ). Although low in abundance, the expansion of T cells in aged CLs (Fig. 6c ; P = 0.0079, two-tailed t -test) may represent the anatomical location underlying prior reports of cytotoxic and double negative T cells accumulation in the aging mouse ovary 34 . Altogether, these data reveal that ovarian aging involves coordinated remodeling of multiple immune niches, pointing to spatially coexisting immune programs that may jointly drive ovarian inflammaging.

### MNGCs define a specialized macrophage fusion pathology in aging ovaries
Among age-expanded immune niches, multinucleated giant cells (MNGCs) emerged as a distinct macrophage-associated pathology. Accumulation of MNGCs is a hallmark of ovarian aging associated with chronic inflammation and fibrosis 8 , 28 , 98 , 99 , visible as fused cellular clusters on H&amp;E sections (Fig. 7a,b and Extended Data Fig. 6a ). Registering adjacent H&amp;E sections to Slide-seq pucks using anatomical landmarks enabled comparing immune spots located within versus outside MNGCs (Fig. 7c , Extended Data Fig. 6b and Methods ), which revealed an enrichment of phagocytic macrophages within MNGCs (Fig. 7d ). Across macrophage subpopulations, those within MNGCs adopted specialized transcriptional programs distinct from the surrounding stroma, including complement- and fusion-associated genes ( Tagln , Acta2, Itgae ) in antigen-presenting macrophages, clearance programs in efferocytic macrophages ( Gpnmb , Mfge8 , Ctsd ) and inflammatory-lipid remodeling signatures in metabolically active macrophages ( Pla2g7 , Lyz2 , Lgals3 ) (Fig. 7e , Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Table 20 ). Together, these findings suggest that MNGCs represent specialized inflammatory fusion niches underlying defective tissue clearance, potentially linking immune dysfunction to fibrotic pathology.

### Aging disrupts interfollicular spatial coupling
Age-associated immune remodeling converged with broader stromal disorganization, suggesting organ-level consequences of inflammaging. Across stromal populations residing outside of follicles and CL, we observed a progressive expansion of surface epithelial and immune populations, accompanied by depletion of steroidogenic stromal cells 7 , 100 – 103 (Fig. 7f , compositional test with scCODA 104 ; Extended Data Fig. 6d ; Supplementary Table 5 ; and Methods ). Thickening of the surface epithelium was independently confirmed by morphometric measurements on adjacent H&amp;E sections (Extended Data Fig. 6e and Methods ). Cell type compositional shifts coincided with transcriptional changes marked by reduced expression of ECM genes and increased metalloproteases that may indicate aberrant ECM remodeling, as well as elevated fibrotic and inflammatory signatures 100 (Fig. 7g , Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Tables 21 and 22 ).

### Discussion
Here we present a near-cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the naturally cycling murine ovary across reproductive ages and show that ovarian aging is characterized by the progressive erosion of multiscale spatiotemporal tissue organization. Across cellular, niche and tissue scales, aging disrupted spatial patterning within follicles, temporal coordination of folliculogenesis and CL turnover, and immune–stromal homeostasis, with changes emerging before cessation of cycling. These findings indicate that reproductive aging can be viewed as a progressive breakdown of tissue-level coordination, rather than solely the depletion of the follicle reserve.
Our findings suggest that the spatial organization of follicles is an elegant mechanism for survival and resource allocation. By compartmentalizing proliferative activity to inner GCs and hormone-sensing, steroidogenic functions to outer GCs positioned near the vasculature and stroma, follicles optimize resource allocation under the energetic constraints of this competitive environment. We hypothesize that successful spatial compartmentalization of GC function during folliculogenesis could contribute to follicular fate, with dominant follicles effectively maintaining functional polarity, whereas less efficient competitors undergo atresia 107 , 108 . More broadly, our findings refine a view of follicular atresia as a heterogeneous process linked to metabolic, immune and tissue remodeling programs, rather than a uniform degenerative endpoint. Although our results suggest a plausible sequence of atresia commitment arising from multiple GC lineages, the specific molecular drivers remain to be experimentally validated 109 – 112 . In aged ovaries, the blurring of developmental and degenerative boundaries points to compromised follicle viability. Whether atretic fate is caused primarily by oocyte-intrinsic cues or by a dysregulated follicular environment remains unclear.

### Estrous cycle staging mice by vaginal cytology
Mice collected at UCSF were staged near-daily for 8 consecutive days using vaginal cytology, as previously described 118 , 119 . A total volume of 100 µl sterile saline (in 20–50 µl increments) was expelled five to ten times with a P200 pipette into the vaginal canal, taking care to avoid touching the vaginal opening with the pipette tip then expelled onto a glass slide and imaged immediately using Nikon Eclipse Ts2 (10× objective) and a Nikon DS Qi2 camera. Broad and Yale mice
Female mice were staged near-daily for 8 consecutive days using vaginal cytology, as previously described 118 , 119 . Briefly, mini-tip flocked nasopharyngeal swabs (VWR SLIN501CS01) were moistened with sterile PBS, and approximately one-fourth of the flocked tip was inserted into the vaginal canal of manually restrained mice. Swabs were rotated five times clockwise and five times counterclockwise and then smeared onto a non-treated glass slide (VWR 16004-422). Slides were air-dried and stained with a 0.1% crystal violet solution (Jorgenson J0322) for 1–2 min. Excess stain was rinsed with PBS and sterile water, and the slides were counterstained with 1% eosin (Jorgenson #J0322A) for 10–20 s. Following the counterstaining step, slides were rinsed again, air-dried completely, examined under a light microscope and imaged with a Leica Aperio VERSA Brightfield, Fluorescence &amp; FISH Digital Pathology Scanner, using the 20× objective.

### In situ transcriptome processing via Slide-seq
Tissue sections were processed and sequenced using Slide-seq v2 as previously described 36 . Slide-seq arrays were purchased from Curio Biosciences (Curio Seeker) or prepared in-house using custom-synthesized barcoded beads functionalized with the sequence 25 (5′TTT_PC_GCCGGTAATACGACTCACTATAGGGCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCTJJJJJJJJTCTTCAGCGTTCCCGAGAJJJJJJNNNNNNNVVT30-3′) with a photocleavable linker (PC), a bead barcode sequence (J, 14 bp), a UMI sequence (NNNNNNNVV, 9 bp) and a poly dT tail. The sample table of all Slide-seq data, denoting the puck origin and other metadata, is in Supplementary Table 2 .

### Initial data processing
Gene expression data of individual samples or pucks were concatenated using an outer join. For spatial data, spatial coordinates were assigned by matching barcodes to puck-specific barcode mapping files. The combined dataset was filtered to retain spots with at least 50 detected genes and 150 UMI counts. For spot clustering and embeddings, all gene expression values were scaled and centered, and the top 5,000 highly variable genes were identified from log-normalized counts across batches using Scanpy’s highly_variable_genes function (batch Key=puck) 124 . Dimensionality reduction was performed by regressing out total UMI counts, followed by principal component analysis (PCA) on highly variable genes. Puck-specific batch effects were corrected using a PyTorch implementation of Harmony 125 , after which a k-nearest-neighbor graph with 10 neighbors was constructed using the top 40 principal components. Unsupervised spot clusters were identified using the Leiden algorithm 126 (resolution = 1.5) and visualized using UMAP 127 , implemented in Scanpy 124 (v1.10.1).

### Projection of additional pucks onto the annotated reference atlas
To incorporate newly generated Slide-seq pucks (young, metestrus) into the reference atlas, raw gene-by-spot matrices were preprocessed as described above, including spatial coordinate assignment and smear removal. To ensure compatibility with the reference atlas, gene sets were harmonized prior to integration by restricting the query AnnData object to the intersection of genes shared between query and reference. The cleaned query data were projected onto the existing atlas using scvi-tools (v1.1.6), leveraging a pretrained SCVI model to infer a shared representation. Latent embeddings for the query were obtained and concatenated with reference embeddings for downstream analysis.

### Subclustering of immune cells and GCs
To refine cell state annotation, we performed iterative subclustering of immune cells and GCs. AnnData objects were subset to populations of interest, normalized to 10,000 transcripts per cell with highly expressed genes down-weighted (max_fraction = 0.05), log-transformed and scaled to unit variance. Highly variable genes were identified using Scanpy’s highly_variable_genes function (flavor = ‘seurat’, batch_key = ‘segment_label’), followed by PCA and neighborhood graph construction. UMAP was used for visualization and Leiden clustering for subcluster identification. DEGs were identified for each subcluster using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (min log fold-change ≥ 1). Marker genes used for annotation were required to be (i) specific to the cluster, (ii) highly expressed within that cluster and (iii) supported by prior literature as having cell-type-defining functional roles.

### Spatial segmentation of oocytes, follicles and CL
Code underlying these analyses can be found in II.2_segmentation.ipynb and II.3_segment_extension.ipynb.
‘Oocyte’ and ‘Oocyte - cumulus’ clusters were initially used as putative oocyte spots to account for uncertainty at cluster boundaries in space. For each puck, a spatial neighborhood graph (radius = 50) was constructed and clustered using Leiden 126 (resolution = 0.1) to define preliminary oocyte segments. ‘Oocyte - cumulus’ spots were subsequently removed, and segments containing fewer than three spots were excluded. Segments were further refined by subclustering, merging and manual curation based on tissue context. Decontamination of cumulus signals from oocytes
To remove residual cumulus contamination from oocytes, NMF 136 was applied iteratively to oocyte spots using scikit-learn 137 ( k = 8 programs). Programs associated with contaminating signals were identified by marker genes, and spots were annotated as contaminants if they either had these programs as their top utilized program or if the program scores reached the following thresholds: Program 1 ( Kctd14 , Slc18a2 , Wt1 ): &gt; 0.4, Program 2 ( Lars2 , Hexb , Cdk8 ): &gt; 0.3, Program 4 ( Inhba , Inhbb , Nap1l5 ): &gt; 0.3, Program 6 ( Col1a2 , Col3a1 , Cfh ): &gt; 0.4 (Supplementary Fig. 3a,b ). Contaminating spots were removed across two rounds of filtering; in the second round, spots with program 1 ( Serpine2 , Ccnd2 , Kctd14 ) as the top program or with a score &gt;0.3 were annotated as contaminants (Supplementary Fig. 3c,d ) and removed from the oocyte segments. Identifying primordial oocytes
To capture small, putatively primordial, oocytes, unassigned ‘Oocyte’ spots or spots expressing Sohlh1 31 , 138 located at least 200 from existing oocyte segment centers were selected. For pucks containing at least two such spots, a neighborhood graph (radius 20 µm) was clustered using Leiden 124 clustering (resolution = 0.1). Segments with less than 2 spots or lacking Sohlh1 expression were excluded. Segmenta

### Analysis of GEPs with pseudotime (DPT)
To investigate transcriptional dynamics during follicle development and atresia, GC GEP usage scores were analyzed along DPT, computed as a unified trajectory across all GC spots. Stage stream plots depict follicle type occupancy along pseudotime, estimated using Gaussian kernel density estimates over 400 grid points and displayed as stacked area plots. Estrous stage occupancy (second row, where available) was computed similarly. GEP heatmaps were generated separately for non-atretic and atretic by binning pseudotime into 500 equal-width intervals and calculating mean GEP usage per bin.
Age-associated differences in GEP usage were tested within each GEP, follicle type and estrous stage using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with cluster-robust standard errors (Usage_k ~ age; young as reference), clustering variance by puck to account for within-puck dependence of spots. Strata lacking both age groups were not estimable. Across all tested GEP × follicle type × stage combinations, P values were adjusted for multiple testing (Benjamini–Hochberg; significance set at FDR &lt; 0.05). Analyses were performed using statsmodels (statsmodels.formula.api.ols, statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests).

### Compositional analysis of cell and segment types
Global cell-type compositional analysis
Cell-type composition was calculated as the fraction of spots assigned to each cell type within each puck, and then averaged across young, middle and old groups. Age-associated compositional changes were tested using scCODA 143 , with young as the reference condition, and ‘Epithelial – oviduct’ as the reference cell type because of its low variability across conditions. Immune subsets were additionally stratified by segment assignments (follicle, CL or stroma if unassigned). CL-associated endothelial cells were analyzed separately from other endothelial cells. Cell-type composition within segments
Within each segment, cell-type composition was calculated as the fraction of spots assigned to each cell type, and then averaged across segment types. To test age-associated differences within follicle types, proportions were transformed using a centered log-ratio and modeled using OLS regression (centered log-ratio ~ age) with cluster-robust standard errors by puck to account for within-sample correlation. As before, P values were adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing (Benjamini–Hochberg; significance, FDR &lt; 0.10). Segment-type composition analysis

### Follicle embedding and trajectory inference using optimal transport
Code for these analyses is in III_segment_OT_1_pca_coretypes.ipynb and III_segment_OT_2_plot_results.ipynb.
Segment-to-segment distance matrix computation
Pairwise distances between all follicle and CL segments in young mice were computed using optimal transport, with each segment represented by its oocyte, granulosa or luteal, and theca spots. For each segment pair, a transport matrix was estimated using the Sinkhorn algorithm implemented in moscot 144 (epsilon = 0, tau_a = 1, tau_b = 1, rank = 20, initializer = k-means, min_iterations = 5, max_iterations = 200). Segment distance was defined as the sum of the element-wise product of the transport matrix and the corresponding cost matrix of the optimal transport problem. Segment embedding and follicle pseudotime
The resulting segment-to-segment distance matrix used as a feature space for embedding. A k-nearest neighbor graph ( k = 15) was constructed from the top 50 PCs and visualized using UMAP. Embeddings were generated for all follicle and CL segments in young mice, as well as follicles alone in young mice as the reference trajectory. DPT 139 was then computed for young follicles using a manually selected root segment. Trajectory projection of follicles from middle-aged and old mice

Code for these analyses is in III.5_nichenet_ageYoung_stageAll_segmentFollicle_withOocyte_byCluster.Rmd and III_segment_OT_2_plot_results_v0.3.ipynb.

### Age-associated differential gene expression analysis
For follicular hormone-response genes, mean expression and s.e.m. were calculated within each follicle type (preantral, antral mitotic, antral luteinizing and atretic), estrous stage (estrus, metestrus) and age group for Amhr2 , Fshr and Lhcgr 8 , 28 , 98 , 99 , 145 . Differential expression between estrous stages was performed using two-sided t -tests. Oocytes and stromal cells

Code for these analyses is in II.5_registration_v0.8_all_pucks.ipynb and III_MNGC_dotplot_v0.1.ipynb.
Annotation of MNGCs in histology sections
Adjacent H&amp;E-stained sections were manually annotated for MNGCs based on pigmentation, size and proximity to growing follicles, as previously described 8 , 28 , 98 , 99 , 146 . Sections were classified as ‘visible MNGCs’ (high density of light brown clusters; n = 19), ‘possible MNGCs’ (lower density or weaker pigmentation; n = 13) or ‘no MNGCs.’ MNGC segmentation in registered spatial transcriptomics data

### Abstract
Throughout the female reproductive lifespan, the ovary undergoes hundreds of cycles of follicle development, ovulation and tissue regeneration. How aging disrupts the coordination of such precise, multicellular interactions across time and space is not well understood. Using Slide-seq, a near-cellular spatial transcriptomics method, here we profile 22 mouse ovaries across the reproductive cycle and chronological ages, capturing 610,620 spots across 69 spatial profiles. We develop a novel segmentation pipeline to examine the multicellular dynamics of 358 oocytes, 668 follicles and 236 corpora lutea to find that aging impairs the spatial and temporal coordination required for folliculogenesis even before reproductive cycles cease. These disruptions are characterized by altered immune cell dynamics, inflammatory signaling and global tissue disorganization, which impair the cyclic remodeling required for ovarian function. Our findings reveal how multicellular niches orchestrate ovarian function and demonstrate that age-related breakdown in tissue organization precedes the end of fertility.
Subject terms: Multicellular systems, Computational biology and bioinformatics, Ageing

### Main
The ovary is a highly dynamic organ that undergoes repeated cycles of phenotypic switching to orchestrate oocyte maturation, ovulation and endocrine signaling throughout the reproductive cycle 1 , 2 . This ‘homeostatic cycling’ occurs approximately 150–650 times in mice and 300–400 times in humans throughout the female reproductive lifespan 3 , 4 . Chronological aging leads to a progressive decline in reproductive function, ultimately culminating in the cessation of these cycles. Here we investigate the molecular interactions underlying this transition, focusing on the depletion of the ovarian reserve, the loss of precision in cellular interactions and the accumulation of tissue-wide inflammation and fibrosis 5 – 10 .
Central to ovarian function are follicles, which are multicellular structures that develop growing oocytes and transform into corpora lutea (CL) after ovulation. Folliculogenesis begins with primordial follicles, consisting of a dormant oocyte encased by flattened granulosa cells (GCs). Follicle activation triggers GC proliferation, first forming preantral follicles that undergo morphological and functional changes to support oocyte growth and then transitioning to the gonadotropin-dependent and steroidogenic antral stage 11 , 12 . Notably, less than 1% of recruited follicles reach ovulation while the rest undergo atresia (that is, controlled follicle death) 13 . After ovulation, follicular remnants transform into the CL, a transient progesterone-producing endocrine structure essential for pregnancy and cycle regulation 12 , 14 . Follicle maturation spans multiple reproductive cycles, approximately 18 days in mice and 375 days in humans, creating an extraordinarily complex tissue environment where dozens (mice) or thousands (humans) of follicles at varying developmental stages share the same physical space with multiple CLs 15 , 16 . The molecular mechanisms coordinating such asynchronous spatiotemporal organization remain poorly defined, underscoring 

### Spatial transcriptomics reveals multicellular organization of the cycling and aging ovary
To characterize the multicellular architecture of the ovary, we generated spatial transcriptomics profiles from mice across three reproductive age groups: young (10–12 weeks), middle-aged (36–40 weeks) and old (52–54 weeks) mice 38 . Mice were harvested during the ovulatory (estrus) and post-ovulatory (metestrus) phases, with active cycling confirmed via longitudinal estrous staging (Fig. 1a , Extended Data Fig. 1a , Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 and Methods ). Unsupervised clustering and post hoc annotation resolved all major ovarian cell populations, including oocytes ( Gdf9 ), multiple GC subtypes, theca cells ( Col1a2 ) and two distinct luteal populations ( Parm1 or Akr1c18 ). We also identified epithelial ( Epcam ), fibroblast ( Pdgfra ), smooth muscle ( Tagln ), immune ( Lyz2 ), endothelial ( Flt1 ) and stromal ( Aldh1a1 ) cells (Fig. 1b–d , Extended Data Fig. 1b , Supplementary Tables 3 – 5 and Supplementary Note). To validate these Slide-seq annotations, we also performed whole-ovary single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq). Although snRNA-seq recovered a consistent set of cell types, it showed a notable loss of oocytes and cumulus cells, underscoring the advantage of our spatial profiling for capturing a more comprehensive ovarian cellular atlas (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d ).
Fig. 1. A spatiotemporal map of the cycling and aging ovary identifies spatial niches driving folliculogenesis.
a , Experimental overview. Mice were staged by vaginal cytology and collected at estrus and metestrus ( n = 22; young 10–12 weeks, middle-aged 36–40 weeks, old 52–54 weeks). Multiple nonadjacent sections per ovary were profiled using Slide-seq, with a minimum gap of 200 µm to avoid resampling the same follicle or CL. Adjacent sections were used for histology. After clustering and cell-type annotation, multicellular segments were defined using an automated segmentation pipeline. b , UMAP of Slide-seq RNA profiles ( n = 610,620 dots at 10 µm resolution) across 69 pucks, colored by post h

### Oocytes follow coordinated transcriptional programs during follicular development
Although oocytes are traditionally viewed as transcriptionally silent storage units for maternal RNA 42 , recent evidence reveals active transcriptional regulation throughout their maturation 43 – 45 . Indeed, our in situ profiling of oocyte transcriptomes showed that canonical oocyte marker genes were differentially expressed across their follicle stages (Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ) 31 , 46 – 48 . Further analysis via non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) revealed five distinct oocyte gene programs across their maturation (Fig. 2d , Methods , Extended Data Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ). Oocyte program 2, characterized by zona pellucida glycoproteins genes Zp2 and Zp3 , was upregulated in primordial and preantral oocytes, suggesting the synthesis of components essential for follicular assembly following primordial activation 49 , 50 . In contrast, oocyte program 4, enriched in Bmp15 and F-box proteins genes ( Fbxw19 , Fbxw21 , Fbxw24 ) encoding components of the SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase complex controlling cell cycle progression 51 , 52 , emerged in mature antral oocytes, reflecting shifts required for meiotic progression. In mature oocytes, we observed a significant increase in oocyte program 0 ( Bcl2l10 , Btg4 , Tcl1 ), signaling readiness for growth following the gonadotropin surge (Fig. 2e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0001 preantral versus antral; two-tailed t -test) 53 – 55 . Conversely, atretic oocytes failed to maintain the expression of these programs, showing a loss of Padi6 expression and a premature induction of oocyte program 0 (Fig. 2a,e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0203 antral versus atretic; two-tailed t -test). Altogether, our findings reveal that oocyte transcription may be dynamically regulated throughout folliculogenesis to govern the switch from oocyte dormancy to maturation.

a , Mean expression (lo

### Molecular programs define spatially organized follicle lifecycles in young ovaries
Next, we investigated how GC states change throughout folliculogenesis. To compare GC organization across hundreds of follicles of varying sizes, we devised a normalized, scaled radial distance from the follicle center. Quantifying GC composition along this radial axis revealed extensive intra-follicle heterogeneity, indicating that transitions between follicle stages are not driven by a synchronized follicle-wide switch, but instead may emerge through the local propagation of changes in cell–cell interactions (Fig. 3a,b , Extended Data Fig. 3a , Supplementary Table 6 and Methods ).
Fig. 3. Spatiotemporal coordination of GCs within the follicular niche.

Lines indicate mean proportion of each subtype across 10 scaled radial bins ( x axis; 0, follicle center; 1, edge); shading, s.e.m. across follicles. Significant monotonic radial trends are indicated (preantral follicles: GC—preantral * P = 0.0283, antral mitotic follicles: GC—antral mitotic * P = 0.0479, GC—antral luteinizing * P = 0.0479, antral luteinizing follicles: GC—antral luteinizing * P = 0.0045, atretic follicles: GC—atretic * P &lt; 0.0001, two-sided Spearman correlation). n = 653 follicles from 22 mice, all ages; follicle counts by type in Supplementary Table 6 . c , Spatial organization of GC cell cycle states. Left: representative spatial plot with cycling (G2M/S, pink) and non-cycling (G1, gray) GCs. Right: mean radial distribution of cycling vs non-cycling GCs ( y axis); shading, s.e.m. across follicles. Significant monotonic trends indicated (cycling: * P &lt; 0.0001, non-cycling: * P &lt; 0.0001, two-sided Spearman correlation; n = 668 follicles). d , Diffusion pseudotime (DPT) across non-atretic

### Aging disrupts the temporal trajectory of GC differentiation and alters atresia progression
Analysis of transcriptional programs across the follicular lifecycle revealed that aging disrupts the coordinated molecular transitions observed across granulosa cell differentiation. In young ovaries, GEP usage across GC trajectories defined by DPT and follicle type follow an ordered progression: GCs in preantral follicles initiate an early development program (GEP9; Wt1, Wnt4 ), progress through proliferative expansion (GEP3; Top2a , Mki67 ) in antral, followed by the induction of follicular dominance (GEP2 and GEP4; Inhbb , Fst ; Esr2 , Greb1l ) and luteinization (GEP1; Lhcgr , Hsd3b1 ) programs heightened at metestrus (Fig. 3h , Extended Data Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Table 12 ). Atretic follicles are characterized by apoptosis-associated programs (GEP10 and GEP11; Thbs1 , Pik3ip1 ; Ghr, Ptprd ) (Fig. 3h , Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 12 ). In contrast, aged ovaries displayed altered timing and intensity of GEPs, indicating a breakdown in the normal sequence of GC state transitions across follicle development (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 3h ). For example, aged antral follicles downregulate the luteinization program (GEP1) (Fig. 3h,i , Extended Data Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Table 12 ). Notably, atretic follicles were the most affected by aging, with decreased canonical apoptosis-associated programs (GEP10 and GEP11) and aberrant upregulation of the ECM remodeling program (GEP6; Col1a2 , Lama2 ), which is typically specific to preantral follicles in young ovaries. These patterns suggest an age-associated shift from regulated to dysregulated remodeling of the follicular niche, resulting in a ‘molecular blurring’ between the boundaries of developmental and degenerative processes.

### Multicellular dynamics and interactions shaping folliculogenesis progression
Folliculogenesis is driven by coordinated interactions across multiple cell types, extending beyond cell-intrinsic granulosa programs. To resolve this higher-order organization (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6 ), we ordered follicle segments from reproductively young mice along a computationally inferred trajectory of folliculogenesis (Fig. 4b,c and Supplementary Table 6 ), visualized in a UMAP embedding (Fig. 4d , Extended Data Fig. 4a , Supplementary Tables 6 and 15 and Methods ). Diffusion pseudotime recapitulated canonical transitions from preantral to antral or atretic follicles (Fig. 4e ), accompanied by progressive shifts in cell type composition (Extended Data Fig. 4b ). To link these compositional changes to intercellular signaling, we applied MultiNicheNet 85 to infer receptor-ligand interactions among oocytes, granulosa, theca and immune cells ( Methods and Extended Data Fig. 4c ). This analysis revealed follicle stage-specific communication patterns, including Gdf9 - Fxyd6 between oocytes and GCs in preantral follicles, Fst - Bmpr1b between granulosa and theca cells in antral follicles, and Apoa4 - Lrp1 within GCs in atretic follicles (Fig. 4f , Supplementary Table 16 and Methods ). The atretic-enriched Apoa4-Lrp1 interaction implicated metabolic reprogramming during follicle regression: Lrp1 regulates lipid transport and glucose metabolism 86 , 87 , whereas Apoa4 promotes lipid handling and facilitates glucose uptake 88 . Notably, LRP1 has been genetically associated with polycystic ovarian syndrome, a disorder characterized by metabolic and endocrine dysfunction 89 . Together, these results indicate that dynamic, stage-specific intercellular signaling coordinates follicle progression.

### Dysregulation of CL clearance with aging may initiate inflammatory remodeling
We next examined whether the dynamics of the post-ovulatory luteal cells are also altered with age. Identification of two spatially segregated luteal cell populations with opposing progesterone regulatory programs suggested a temporal phenotypic switch during the luteal lifecycle. Parm1 -enriched CLs (‘CL – Parm1’) express progesterone synthesis genes, contain vascular endothelial cells, are enriched at estrus and consist of histologically smaller cells 92 , 93 , features consistent with newly formed, hormonally active CLs 14 , 32 , 94 – 96 . In contrast, Akr1c18 -enriched CLs (‘CL – Akr1c18’) express the luteal regression marker Ptgfr , are infiltrated by immune cells, are more frequent at metestrus and contain histologically larger cells 92 , 93 , features consistent with luteolysis and regression (Fig. 5a–c , Extended Data Fig. 5a–f and Supplementary Tables 4 , 6 and 17 ) 96 . In aged ovaries, although these transcriptional distinctions between luteal subtypes were preserved (Extended Data Fig. 5g ), Akr1c18 CLs were significantly accumulated at estrus compared to young ovaries (Fig. 5b , P = 0.0055, two-tailed t -test; Supplementary Table 17 ), suggesting failed timely clearance. Because timely CL regression and the accompanying drop in progesterone are required to initiate the next cycle 14 , 95 , 97 , persistence of these degenerating CLs likely disrupts progesterone homeostasis, potentially impairing cycle progression 1 , 11 .
